summary: BBN explains why sites may see messages from IMPs or hosts they thought did not exist: new IMPs are tested on the network at BBN before delivery, sometimes with another number. Hosts do not need to update their tables.

plainLanguage.summary: BBN sometimes tested new IMPs on the network before sending them to their permanent sites. During a test, an IMP could use a number different from the one it would later have, so sites did not need to change their host tables.

subtitle: Why temporary IMP tests can produce unfamiliar host numbers

tldr.problem: Network sites may see reset messages from an IMP or host whose number they do not recognize.
tldr.mechanism: BBN explains that it tests new IMPs on the ARPANET before delivery, sometimes using a temporary number already assigned elsewhere.
tldr.outcome: Sites should not change host tables for these tests; BBN says to wait for official notice before making such changes.

today: RFC 305 is a notice about how BBN tested new IMPs on the ARPANET. It explains that test messages did not by themselves call for changes to host tables.

sections.title: Testing New IMPs on the Network
sections.content: BBN says that it almost always tested new IMPs on the ARPANET before delivering them to their intended sites. As a result, a site might receive a connection request or reset message from an IMP or host it did not expect to exist yet.
sections.plainLanguage: BBN tested new network equipment before shipping it to its assigned site. Other sites could see messages from that equipment during the test.

sections.title: Temporary Numbers During Testing
sections.content:
A test IMP could announce a number different from the number planned for its permanent installation. The example is a TIP intended for ETAC, where IMP number 20 was already in use. BBN tested it as number 22, which produced reset messages with network address 150.

The temporary number explained why the messages did not match the official host information.
sections.plainLanguage: A test unit could use a number that belonged to another site because its final number was already in use. That could make its network messages look unfamiliar.

sections.title: When to Change Host Tables
sections.content: BBN answers that sites do not need to update their host tables because of these test messages. Hosts may ignore or close connections from test IMPs. The notice says host tables should be changed only after official notification from BBN, either through an RFC or an update to Appendix A of BBN Report 1822.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not change a host table just because a test unit sends a message. Wait for BBN's official notice before changing it.
